tip: Background description in imperfeito: 'fazia calor e o sol brilhava' sets the scene for 'saímos' (event).
'Fazer besteira' means to do something dumb; 'besteira' comes from 'besta' (beast).
'Disse' covers both 'I said' and 'he/she said'; only the pronoun ('eu' vs 'ele') tells them apart.
'Fazer as pazes' means to make up/reconcile after a fight. Always plural: 'as pazes', never 'a paz' in this expression.
'Foram' means both 'went' and 'were'; the adjective after it, 'foram felizes', marks it as 'were' here.
'Vocês' is the plural 'you' everywhere; Portugal's older 'vós' still shows up in writing but is mostly gone from speech.
'Viram' means 'saw'; add an e and you get 'vieram', 'came'. One letter separates them.
'Vir' (to come) becomes 'veio' (he/she came). Don't confuse it with 'viu', from 'ver' (to see).
Reported speech often keeps the original tense: 'disse que vai' is 'said she will', where English usually shifts to 'would'.
'Vi' is 'I saw', as in 'vi um acidente'; don't mix it up with 'vim', 'I came'. One letter apart.
'Pôs' is the past of 'pôr', 'put'; in casual Brazilian speech people often reach for 'colocar' instead ('colocou').
'Estava cheio' (imperfeito, description) + 'chegamos' (perfeito, event). Scene + arrival pattern.
'Concurso' in Brazil refers to competitive civil service exams. Passing one is a big achievement and usually leads to a stable government job.
'Pamonha' is a traditional Brazilian snack made from fresh corn wrapped in corn husks. Very popular in the countryside and during 'festas juninas'.
'Por' for exchange/substitution: 'trocar A por B' = to exchange A for B.
'Enquanto' (while) takes the imperfect for background action ('jantava'); the main event uses the simple past ('contou').
'Sabia' (imperfeito, state of not knowing) + 'vi' (perfeito, moment of seeing). Discovery interrupted a state.
'Arrepender-se de' means 'to regret'. This verb is always reflexive in standard Portuguese – there's no non-reflexive form.
'Te falei' = I told you: 'te' is the informal object pronoun. Brazilians pair 'te' with 'você' even though it belongs to 'tu'.
'Brincar' takes 'de' before a game: 'brincava de esconde-esconde', literally 'played of' hide and seek.
'Sonhar' takes 'em' before a verb, not 'de': 'sonhava em morar'. English 'dream of' can push you to the wrong preposition.
'Te' as direct object: 'não te entendi' = I didn't understand you. Pronoun before verb in negatives.
'Indicar' looks like 'indicate' but often means recommend: 'me indicou um bom restaurante' is 'suggested a good restaurant to me'.
'Antes de' takes an infinitive where English uses -ing: 'antes de mudar' is 'before switching', not 'before to switch'.
Portuguese questions need no 'do' or 'did': 'quem mandou' is just 'who sent', the plain past-tense verb carrying the question alone.
'Chamar-se' literally means 'to call oneself'. 'Me chamo Lucas' = I call myself Lucas. The most basic reflexive verb you'll learn.
'Orgulhar-se' takes 'de' for what you are proud of: 'orgulha dos filhos', where 'dos' is 'de' plus 'os'.
'A gente' means 'we' in speech but takes a third-person singular verb: 'esperou', not 'esperamos'.
'Sem que' always takes the subjunctive: 'sem que ninguém perceba', where 'perceba' is the subjunctive of 'perceber'.
'Para variar' is a set phrase meaning 'for a change', usually said with irony about something predictable.
